content:
Hello!
I'm preparing to write an article reviewing Lean. I'm currently asking questions and gathering material.

I have a question: which is better at the early stage of development: tests or simple proofs?
I'm absolutely certain that we need tests for complex functions early on, since they undergo refactoring.

But there are also small, simple functions that we probably won't change very often!

What about them? Which is more effective: tests or invariant proofs? Or would both be useful?

I know for a fact that Lean allows you to check invariants by enumerating variations. Looking for counterexamples. Could this be considered a replacement for tests? Not even a replacement, just tests.
You've seen #guard, right? These are useful for verifying that individual functions behave as expected now and in the future.

Yes, I've seen. But #guard is one of many ways to write test.
How to understand, what will be simpler: test or proof?

To me this sounds very domain- or project-dependent. I almost never write tests when my main goal is proving something. But when my main goal is to actually run code then writing tests early on is more natural.

Seconding this. There's a kinda Pareto frontier spectrum going from [instruction-level Hoare triples] to [method-level data invariants and pre/post conditions] to [noncompositional "these specific kinds of bugs don't happen"] and [scenario based examples], which have different amounts of coding effort, specification effort, flexibility under change, etc

if "what should this section of code do?" changes every week because of evolving business requirements then a lot of the theorem statements, not just their proofs, are going to become obsolete quickly
Proofs can be reused in other proofs. If the goal it to prove something "bigger" in the end, having an "API of theorems" describing crucial properties of all definitions will be a huge help.

Fair point. If I replace a Dijkstra's with a Floyd-Warshall there will in fact be a lot of common theorems required to establish and eliminate loop invariants, even if the loop invariants are very different

(The worst case I was thinking about was where the definitions themselves keep shifting, e.g. taking "∀ P, {¬ (user, company) ∈ Admin ∧ P} run {P}" and replacing the precondition with "unless the current API key-ACLs bundle belongs to a user who has 2FA'd in the last 24h, and, there exists a transitive path (user, ?team, ?workspace, resource) which lifts to a path with ≥ Mod permission on the Permissions graph" while having deprecated the concept of "company" entirely)
as Malvin said, very project dependent

If you're talking about, say, some code for a program that does a clearly defined thing (e.g. waterstamp a PNG with a Mersenne prime) then you can absolutely be writing high-level simple proofs from the start. Things like "if module X does Y, and module Z does W, then combining them in this way gives result Ω."

With system design you'd often start by modularising — as in encapsulation, Single Responsibility Principle, typeclass API design — and the way the pieces interact (hopefully!) have less churn than individual complex methods/functions

(if your review needs citations i'd point to Wirth 1971 https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/362575.362577 and Liskov&Zilles 1974
https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/942572.807045 for the evolution of these ideas)

you can already have proofs at this stage! the proofs are about how big components of the program fit together. "this function returns a Mersenne prime"; "this function waterstamps a base-10 number X onto a bitmap of width ≥ 20*log_10(X)" ⊢ "this new function waterstamps a Mersenne prime onto a bitmap of width ≥ 640".

Filipp said:

I have a question: which is better at the early stage of development: tests or simple proofs?
I'm absolutely certain that we need tests for complex functions early on, since they undergo refactoring.

But there are also small, simple functions that we probably won't change very often!

What about them? Which is more effective: tests or invariant proofs? Or would both be useful?

For the small simple functions that won't change... if I understand correctly, many of these are "pure", or at least "idempotent", functions (ie no side effects).
These are worth proving things about. Even if you don't use them, you'll probably use something very similar, and as Adomas says the "API of theorems" will be useful here
you can start with the O(n) Fibonacci numbers, replace them with an O(lg n) Fibonacci implementation, and reuse all the results you already have

Filipp said:

I know for a fact that Lean allows you to check invariants by enumerating variations. Looking for counterexamples. Could this be considered a replacement for tests? Not even a replacement, just tests.

Plausible , yes? It may be helpful to separate "property based testing" (like Plausible) from other forms of testing like "unit testing"
property based testing can be very helpful while the code is being refactored a lot

writing those tests force you to say what the code is supposed to do. E.g. "this function waterstamps a base-10 number X onto a bitmap of width ≥ 20*log_10(X)", the 'specification' from your big picture architecture
but sometimes the code's main purpose is "do this small step as part of a bigger function", and in those cases you may want to use proofs instead

one question you could ask is, "why might this code/function be refactored?"
( :warning: everything I'm saying is personal opinion but especially this: :warning:)

  • if you might change the implementation, but you probably won't change the 'purpose' of the code, it might be a candidate for property-based testing
  • if the code is so small you're going to replace it instead of refactoring it, it might be a candidate for theorems or for unit tests
  • if the code only glues different APIs together, it's a good candidate for theorems
